title: Karp's Twenty-One NP-Complete Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Karp's 1972 paper showed that twenty-one natural combinatorial problems, including clique, vertex cover, and Hamiltonian cycle, are NP-complete.
short: A single reduction from SAT launched the study of NP-completeness.
long: A single reduction from SAT launched the study of NP-completeness. Karp's list demonstrated that NP-completeness is ubiquitous rather than an artifact of logic.
proof: Each listed problem is in NP and admits a polynomial reduction from a previously established NP-complete problem.
consequence: It established the modern practice of proving hardness by chains of reductions.

title: The Polynomial Hierarchy
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The polynomial hierarchy consists of levels Σᵖₖ, Πᵖₖ, and Δᵖₖ obtained by alternating existential and universal polynomial-time quantifiers, with NP as its first existential level.
short: Alternation of guesses builds a ladder above NP and co-NP.
long: Alternation of guesses builds a ladder above NP and co-NP. The hierarchy is contained in PSPACE, and whether it is strict is a major open question.
proof: Define levels inductively with oracle machines: Σᵖ_{k+1} = NP^{Σᵖₖ} and Πᵖ_{k+1} = coNP^{Σᵖₖ}.
consequence: It organizes a wide range of problems by their quantifier structure.

title: PH Collapses If NP Equals co-NP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If NP equals co-NP then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to NP.
short: One collapse at the bottom level topples the entire hierarchy.
long: One collapse at the bottom level topples the entire hierarchy. More generally, if two consecutive levels coincide the hierarchy collapses to that level.
proof: Inductively alternate quantifiers: because NP predicates are closed under universal quantification when NP equals co-NP, all higher levels collapse.
consequence: It explains why NP versus co-NP is a central question.

title: The Class PSPACE
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: PSPACE is the class of decision problems solvable by a Turing machine using an amount of memory bounded by a polynomial in the input length, with no restriction on running time.
short: Space is the scarce resource, and time may be enormous.
long: Space is the scarce resource, and time may be enormous. A polynomial-space machine can run for exponential time, so PSPACE is much larger than P.
proof: Definition; the model requires a read-only input tape so that measured space excludes the input.
consequence: PSPACE contains NP and the polynomial hierarchy.

title: Quantified Boolean Formulas Are PSPACE-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Deciding the truth of a fully quantified Boolean formula is complete for PSPACE.
short: Quantifier alternation over Boolean variables captures polynomial space.
long: Quantifier alternation over Boolean variables captures polynomial space. The problem generalizes SAT by allowing universal quantifiers interleaved with existential ones.
proof: Evaluate the quantifier tree recursively in polynomial space; conversely, simulate a polynomial-space machine's accepting computation by a quantified formula.
consequence: QBF is the canonical complete problem for PSPACE.

title: Savitch's Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every language accepted by a nondeterministic machine in space s(n) is accepted by a deterministic machine in space s(n) squared.
short: Nondeterminism saves at most a quadratic factor of space.
long: Nondeterminism saves at most a quadratic factor of space. In particular nondeterministic polynomial space equals deterministic polynomial space.
proof: Use a recursive reachability algorithm that tests whether an accepting configuration is reachable within a bounded number of steps via a midpoint configuration.
consequence: It is a rare case where nondeterminism can be eliminated with only polynomial overhead.

title: The Class L of Logarithmic Space
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: L is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine using O(log n) workspace besides a read-only input tape.
short: Logarithmic space means only enough memory to store a few pointers.
long: Logarithmic space means only enough memory to store a few pointers. Containing the input on a separate read-only tape is essential; otherwise reading the input would already require linear space.
proof: Definition with the standard multi-tape machine model.
consequence: L is a small but surprisingly expressive class, containing undirected reachability.

title: The Class NL
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NL is the class of problems solvable by a nondeterministic Turing machine using logarithmic workspace.
short: Guessing a path needs only a logarithmic-length counter.
long: Guessing a path needs only a logarithmic-length counter. Directed reachability is the canonical NL problem because a path can be guessed one vertex at a time.
proof: A nondeterministic logspace machine guesses a path vertex by vertex, storing only the current vertex and a counter.
consequence: NL sits between L and P and equals its own complement.

title: Directed Reachability Is NL-Complete
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The problem of deciding whether a vertex t is reachable from a vertex s in a directed graph is complete for NL under logarithmic-space reductions.
short: Any logarithmic-space computation can be viewed as a reachability question.
long: Any logarithmic-space computation can be viewed as a reachability question. The computation graph of a logspace machine has polynomially many configurations, each describable in logspace.
proof: Reachability is in NL by guessing the path; any NL computation reduces to reachability on its configuration graph.
consequence: It gives a concrete focus for studying the power of nondeterministic logspace.

title: Immerman–Szelepcsényi Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NL is closed under complement, so NL equals co-NL.
short: Nondeterministic logspace can count its way to a no answer.
long: Nondeterministic logspace can count its way to a no answer. This contrasts with deterministic logspace, where L versus co-L was unknown for a long time and is now known to be equal as well.
proof: Inductively guess and verify the number of vertices reachable within k steps, using certificates for non-reachability at each stage.
consequence: It is a landmark result showing that nondeterminism and complementation can coexist in small space.

title: Undirected Connectivity Lies in Logspace
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Undirected s-t connectivity can be solved deterministically using only logarithmic space.
short: Reingold derandomized the walk-based algorithm using expander graphs.
long: Reingold derandomized the walk-based algorithm using expander graphs. The result settled a long-standing question and completed the equality L = SL, where SL is the symmetric logspace class.
proof: Replace the random walk by a deterministic traversal of a power graph built from constant-degree expanders.
consequence: It is a rare example of a complete derandomization result.

title: The Time Hierarchy Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: For every time-constructible function t, the class DTIME(t(n)) is strictly contained in DTIME(t(n)² log t(n)).
short: More time lets a machine solve strictly more problems.
long: More time lets a machine solve strictly more problems. A convenient corollary is that DTIME(nᵏ) is strictly contained in DTIME(nᵏ⁺¹).
proof: Diagonalize: a machine in the larger class simulates all machines in the smaller class on their own descriptions and flips each answer.
consequence: It guarantees that complexity classes defined by time do not all coincide.

title: The Space Hierarchy Theorem
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If s is little-o of S and S is space-constructible, then DSPACE(s(n)) is strictly contained in DSPACE(S(n)).
short: Extra memory gives strictly more computational power.
long: Extra memory gives strictly more computational power. The theorem applies to all standard space bounds and implies, for example, that L is strictly smaller than PSPACE.
proof: Diagonalization with a simulator that uses a delimiter to mark how much space a simulated machine is allowed.
consequence: It prevents the space hierarchy from collapsing.

title: Ladner's Theorem and NP-Intermediate Problems
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If P differs from NP, then there exist languages in NP that are neither in P nor NP-complete.
short: The NP landscape has intermediate rungs if P and NP differ.
long: The NP landscape has intermediate rungs if P and NP differ. The construction uses delayed diagonalization against both all polynomial-time machines and all NP-completeness reductions.
proof: Build a language that interpolates between a simple set and SAT by deciding membership based on a slowly growing time threshold.
consequence: It shows NP-completeness is not the only alternative to tractability.

title: The Class BPP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: BPP is the class of problems decidable in polynomial time by a randomized algorithm with error probability at most one third on every input.
short: Probability of a wrong answer can be made tiny by repetition.
long: Probability of a wrong answer can be made tiny by repetition. The error bound is arbitrary: majority voting reduces a constant gap to exponentially small failure.
proof: Run the algorithm independently O(k) times and output the majority answer; apply the Chernoff bound.
consequence: BPP models efficient randomized computation in practice.

title: BPP Lies in the Polynomial Hierarchy
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: Every language in BPP belongs to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, indeed to the intersection of Σᵖ₂ and Πᵖ₂.
short: Randomness can be simulated by small circuits with quantifiers.
long: Randomness can be simulated by small circuits with quantifiers. This gives evidence that randomized polynomial time is not much more powerful than deterministic polynomial time.
proof: Cover most random strings by a small family of translates using a counting argument, then express acceptance with two quantifier blocks.
consequence: It links derandomization with circuit lower bounds.

title: RP and co-RP One-Sided Error
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: RP is the class where yes instances are accepted with probability at least one half and no instances are never accepted; co-RP reverses the roles.
short: One-sided error means a positive answer can be trusted.
long: One-sided error means a positive answer can be trusted. Primality's Miller–Rabin test puts compositeness in RP (under a deterministic variant).
proof: Amplify each class by repetition; a machine that detects a certificate for either answer gives zero-error expected polynomial time.
consequence: One-sided algorithms are especially useful when false positives are harmless.

title: ZPP and Zero-Error Randomized Time
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: ZPP is the class of problems solvable by a randomized algorithm that never outputs a wrong answer and runs in expected polynomial time.
short: Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have variable running time.
long: Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have variable running time. They contrast with Monte Carlo algorithms in BPP, which have fixed time but a small error probability.
proof: Run an RP algorithm and a co-RP algorithm in parallel until one produces a certified answer.
consequence: It identifies the sweet spot where randomness never compromises correctness.

title: The Class PP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: PP is the class of languages accepted by a polynomial-time randomized machine with probability greater than one half exactly on yes instances.
short: Majority vote defines a surprisingly powerful class.
long: Majority vote defines a surprisingly powerful class. Unlike BPP, the gap from one half may be exponentially small, so error cannot be amplified efficiently.
proof: Definition; note that PP contains NP, because an NP witness can be guessed with probability exponential in the witness length.
consequence: PP is much larger than BPP and contains the entire polynomial hierarchy in relatable forms.

title: The Counting Class #P
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: #P is the class of functions counting the accepting paths of a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine; counting satisfying assignments of a Boolean formula is #P-complete.
short: Counting solutions is harder than deciding whether one exists.
long: Counting solutions is harder than deciding whether one exists. A parsimonious reduction preserves the exact number of solutions, so NP-hardness does not automatically give #P-hardness.
proof: The number of accepting computations of an NP machine is a #P function; SAT's counting version is complete under parsimonious reductions.
consequence: It underpins the complexity of approximate counting and statistical inference.

title: The Schwartz–Zippel Lemma
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: If p is a nonzero polynomial of total degree d over a field and r is chosen uniformly from a finite set S, then the probability that p(r) equals zero is at most d divided by the size of S.
short: Random evaluation detects a nonzero polynomial with high probability.
long: Random evaluation detects a nonzero polynomial with high probability. It works for multivariate polynomials and requires only that the evaluation points be distinct field elements.
proof: Induct on the number of variables and degree, factoring p by a linear factor when it vanishes on a slice.
consequence: It is the workhorse of randomized polynomial identity testing.

title: Interactive Proofs Equal PSPACE
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The class IP of languages with polynomial-time probabilistic verifiers interacting with an all-powerful prover equals PSPACE.
short: Dialogue with a prover captures all polynomial-space computation.
long: Dialogue with a prover captures all polynomial-space computation. The verifier uses private randomness and the prover tries to convince it of membership; soundness must hold against dishonest provers.
proof: Arithmetize a quantified Boolean formula into a low-degree polynomial and use the sum-check protocol to verify its value recursively.
consequence: It is one of the most striking characterizations in complexity theory.

title: Two-Prover Interactive Proofs and NEXP
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: The class MIP of languages with polynomial-time verifiers interacting with two noncommunicating provers equals NEXP.
short: Forbidding provers from talking makes interactive proofs much stronger.
long: Forbidding provers from talking makes interactive proofs much stronger. The verifier can cross-check answers from the two provers, enforcing global consistency that a single prover cannot be forced to satisfy.
proof: Babai, Fortnow, and Lund used low-degree tests and self-correction to encode exponential-time computations into pairs of oracles.
consequence: It explains the power of multiprover protocols and underlies probabilistically checkable proofs.

title: Arthur–Merlin Protocols and Public Coins
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: AM is the class of languages with constant-round interactive proofs in which the verifier's random choices are public; AM is contained in the second level of the polynomial hierarchy.
short: Public randomness can be traded for nondeterminism plus bounded error.
long: Public randomness can be traded for nondeterminism plus bounded error. A constant-round public-coin protocol can be viewed as a Merlin message checked by a probabilistic Arthur.
proof: Guess a likely transcript and use a covering argument to verify that many verifier random strings accept it.
consequence: It connects interactive proofs with classical complexity classes.

title: The Parallel Class NC
subject: Complexity Theory
statement: NC is the class of problems solvable in polylogarithmic time using polynomially many processors on a parallel random-access machine.
latex: NCᵏ: time O(logᵏ n), polynomial processors
short: NC captures problems that are efficiently parallelizable.
long: NC captures problems that are efficiently parallelizable. The levels NCᵏ correspond to different polylogarithmic time bounds; NC is the union over all k.
proof: Definition with the PRAM model allowing concurrent reads and exclusive or concurrent writes.
consequence: It provides a theoretical target for parallel algorithm design.
